stem_html:
The playwright's revisions to the second act are ______: not one line is cut, and the order of two speeches is reversed, after which the ending means something else.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "minimal but consequential"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "extensive", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "reluctant", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "unfinished", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A colon with two clauses often wants a two-part answer.
  • Size and effect are separate axes.
  • Reversing two speeches is a small edit with a large result.

Why A is right The colon gives both halves at once: “not one line is cut”, which is the smallness, and an ending that means something else, which is the consequence.

Why B is wrong Extensive contradicts the first half of the colon.

Why C is wrong Reluctance is an attitude, and the sentence describes the revisions themselves.

Why D is wrong Nothing says the revisions are incomplete; the new ending is achieved.

stem_html:
Rather than resolving the dispute, the arbitrator's ruling ______ it, giving each side a sentence it could quote and neither side a decision it could act on.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "prolonged"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "settled", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "exposed", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "simplified", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “Rather than X” requires not-X.
  • Read the two clauses after the comma; they define the effect.
  • One choice is X wearing a different word.

Why A is right A ruling giving “each side a sentence it could quote and neither side a decision” it could act on leaves the dispute running, which is what “rather than resolving the dispute” requires.

Why B is wrong Settled is a synonym for resolving, which the sentence rules out.

Why C is wrong Exposing would mean revealing something hidden, and the ruling adds nothing to what was known.

Why D is wrong The ruling made the dispute harder to end, not easier to understand.

stem_html:
The biography is ______ about its subject's finances: the sources exist, the author has read them, and the chapters covering the years they document say nothing at all.

Which choice completes the text with the most logical and precise word or phrase?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "conspicuously silent"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "poorly informed", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "openly hostile", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "exhaustive", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The colon exists to rule out the easy reading.
  • Not saying is different from not knowing.
  • Silence with knowledge behind it is conspicuous.

Why A is right The colon rules out ignorance — “the sources exist, the author has read them” — and reports an omission, which makes the silence noticeable rather than accidental.

Why B is wrong The colon says the author has read the sources, so ignorance is excluded.

Why C is wrong Hostility would require the biography to say something unkind, and it says nothing.

Why D is wrong Exhaustive is the opposite of chapters that say nothing at all.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2018 article about shipping containers.

The container was not invented to move goods. It was invented to stop them being stolen, and the man who patented it was a trucking operator tired of paying for pilferage on the docks. That the sealed box also cut loading time from days to hours was noticed later, by other people, and it is the only thing anyone remembers about it now.

Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "To distinguish an invention's original motive from the effect it is now remembered for."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "To explain how shipping containers reduced theft on the docks.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "To argue that the container's inventor deserves more credit than he receives.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "To describe the process by which cargo was loaded before containers.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Purpose is the contrast, not either side of it.
  • The closing clause names what the text is about.
  • Half the contrast is the classic wrong answer.

Why A is right The text sets the patented purpose against the remembered one and closes on the gap: the loading gain “is the only thing anyone remembers about it now”.

Why B is wrong Theft is one half of the contrast, not the point of the whole.

Why C is wrong No claim about credit is made; the inventor's motive is reported, not defended.

Why D is wrong Loading is mentioned only as the effect, never described as a process.

The recordist waits for the aeroplane to pass and then presses record, and the resulting file is called clean. But the birds have been singing over engines all their lives, and a species that has raised its pitch to be heard above traffic sings the way it does because of what the recordist edits out. The clean file is a portrait of an animal with its cause removed.

Which choice best describes the function of the underlined portion in the text as a whole?

explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “But” at the head of a clause usually opens the objection.
  • Check whether the rest of the passage develops the clause.
  • Look at where the detail in a wrong choice actually sits.

Wolves reintroduced to the valley changed the vegetation along its streams. Where wolves hunt, elk browse less in the open, and willow and aspen have returned to banks that were bare for sixty years.

Text 2

Beaver were reintroduced in the same decade, and a beaver dam raises the water table for hundreds of metres upstream. Willow returns where the ground is wet whether or not anything is hunting the elk. Two treatments were applied at once, and the valley cannot tell us which one the willows answered.

Based on the texts, how would the author of Text 2 most likely respond to the explanation offered in Text 1?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "By noting that a second change was made at the same time, so the observation cannot single out the wolves."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "By denying that willow and aspen have returned to the valley's stream banks.", "trap": "too-extreme"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "By arguing that elk browsing has no effect on streamside vegetation.", "trap": "too-extreme"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "By concluding that beaver rather than wolves caused the vegetation to return.", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The last sentence refuses to name a cause.
  • Do not upgrade “cannot tell” to “it was the other one”.

Why A is right Text 2 accepts the recovery and points to a confound: “two treatments were applied at once, and the valley cannot tell us which one the willows answered”.

Why B is wrong Text 2 takes the return of willow as given; it disputes the cause.

Why C is wrong Text 2 never denies that browsing matters, only that browsing is shown to be the cause here.

stem_html: A linguist proposed that a set of loanwords entered the language through trade rather than through conquest, on the grounds that trade borrowings cluster in the vocabulary of goods while conquest borrowings reach law and government as well. Which finding, if true, would most directly support the linguist's proposal?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Of the 340 borrowed words, 318 name commodities, weights or containers, and not one appears in the surviving legal or administrative vocabulary."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "The borrowed words entered the language over a period of about eighty years.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "The two peoples are known to have traded with each other for several centuries.", "trap": "true-but-irrelevant"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Some of the borrowed words also occur in three neighbouring languages.", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The claim supplies its own test; find the finding that runs it.
  • The absence in law is as load-bearing as the presence in goods.
  • Contact alone is consistent with both explanations.

Why A is right The linguist's own test is where the borrowings land, since “trade borrowings cluster in the vocabulary of goods while conquest borrowings reach law and government”. A 318-of-340 commodity cluster with an empty legal vocabulary is that test passed.

Why B is wrong A duration says nothing about which domain the words entered.

Why C is wrong Trade contact is compatible with conquest as well; it does not discriminate.

Why D is wrong Spread across neighbours concerns diffusion, not the domain of the vocabulary.

stem_html: A team claimed that a coral's pale colour in warm water reflects the loss of its algae rather than a change in the coral's own pigment. Which finding, if true, would most strongly support the team's claim?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Algal cell counts in the pale tissue were a twentieth of those in the coloured tissue, while the coral's own pigment proteins were present at the same concentration in both."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Corals in warm water are paler than corals in cool water.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Pale corals recover their colour within weeks when returned to cool water.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "The coral's pigment proteins are known to be sensitive to temperature.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Two candidate causes need one measured and the other controlled.
  • Restating the observation supports neither side.
  • Reversibility is not attribution.

Why A is right The claim is that the pale colour “reflects the loss of its algae rather than a change in the coral's own pigment”, so the finding has to move one source and hold the other. Algae down twentyfold with pigment unchanged does both.

Why B is wrong This restates the phenomenon and leaves its cause open.

Why C is wrong Recovery shows the change is reversible, not which component changed.

Why D is wrong This supports the explanation the team rejects.

stem_html: In her story collection Ninth Ward, Delphine Okoro writes about a city after a flood in a way that treats rebuilding as an act of forgetting rather than of recovery. Which quotation from a fictional story would best illustrate this claim?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "“They raised the new houses a metre higher and painted over the line the water left, and within a year the children were asking what the line had been.”"}, {"letter": "B", "content": "“They raised the new houses a metre higher, because the water had come to the window sills and might come again.”", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "“Nobody in the ward could speak of the flood without stopping halfway through the sentence.”", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "“The city rebuilt slowly, street by street, and it took eleven years.”", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Illustrate means the quotation must enact the claim.
  • Forgetting has to be produced by the rebuilding, not merely coexist with it.
  • The reverse of the claim is always on offer.

Why A is right The claim is that the stories treat “rebuilding as an act of forgetting rather than of recovery”. Here the rebuilding erases the record — the line is painted over — and the erasure produces forgetting within a year.

Why B is wrong This rebuilding is explicitly done in memory of the flood, which is the opposite.

Why C is wrong This is about the difficulty of speaking, and nothing is rebuilt in it.

Why D is wrong A fact about the pace of reconstruction carries no attitude to memory.

The following text is adapted from a 2019 article about medieval account books.

Historians once read a manor's account book for its totals. The totals are the least reliable part: they were copied forward, sometimes for decades, from a figure nobody rechecked. The interesting entries are the corrections in the margin, which record what the steward noticed and when, and they cannot have been copied because there was nothing yet to copy.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "The marginal corrections in a manor's accounts are better evidence than the totals historians used to rely on."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Medieval account books frequently contain arithmetical errors.", "trap": "half-right"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Stewards were responsible for checking the accuracy of a manor's accounts.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Historians should stop using medieval account books as sources.", "trap": "too-extreme"}]

Traps in this question

  • A demotion plus a promotion is one idea, not two.
  • Keep both halves in the answer.
  • Redirecting is not rejecting.

Why A is right The passage demotes the totals and promotes the margins, which “cannot have been copied because there was nothing yet to copy”.

Why C is wrong The steward is a detail inside the argument about the margins.

stem_html:
The following text is adapted from a 2021 essay on urban birdsong.

A sparrow in the city sings a narrower song than a sparrow in the woods, and the usual explanation is traffic: high frequencies carry over engine noise and low ones do not. But city sparrows sing the narrow song at four in the morning, when the streets are empty, and young birds raised in silence sing it too if they were reared by city parents. Whatever narrows the song, it is no longer the noise that started it.

Which choice best states the main idea of the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "A trait that began as a response to noise now persists independently of the noise."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "Traffic noise is the reason city sparrows sing a narrower song than woodland sparrows.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "Young sparrows learn their songs from the adults that rear them.", "trap": "wrong-part-of-passage"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "City sparrows sing earlier in the morning than woodland sparrows do.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • “But” marks where the main idea begins.
  • The last sentence usually states it.
  • The explanation being complicated is the top distractor.

Why A is right Two observations detach the song from the noise, and the closing sentence says so: “it is no longer the noise that started it”.

Why B is wrong That is the explanation the passage sets up in order to complicate.

Why C is wrong The rearing experiment is evidence, not the point.

Why D is wrong The four o'clock detail marks an absence of traffic, not a comparison of schedules.

stem_html:
A chain of clinics moved half its appointment reminders from post to text message and left the other half on post. Missed appointments fell in the texted group and held steady in the posted group. The two groups were drawn from the same patient list at random, and the reminder was sent the same number of days ahead in both. Because the timing and the patients were matched, the drop in missed appointments ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "is most plausibly attributed to the change in how the reminder was delivered."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "shows that patients prefer text messages to letters.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "would have been larger had the reminders been sent earlier.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "proves that postal reminders have no effect at all.", "trap": "too-extreme"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Everything matched but one thing names the cause.
  • Behaviour is not preference.
  • Steady is not zero.

Why A is right Random assignment and matched lead time leave delivery as the only thing that differed, and the passage says “the timing and the patients were matched”.

Why B is wrong Attendance is behaviour, not a stated preference.

Why C is wrong No reminder was sent at a different lead time, so nothing supports the comparison.

Why D is wrong The posted group held steady rather than failing; no baseline without reminders was measured.

stem_html:
A glassblower found that a batch of bottles cracked on cooling while an earlier batch from the same furnace, the same sand and the same day did not. The cracked batch had been moved to the annealing oven in four minutes; the earlier one, in under one. Since everything but the transfer time was held constant, the cracking ______

Which choice most logically completes the text?

explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • A shared factor cannot explain a difference.
  • Find the one variable that moved.
  • The choices name the controls back at you.

Why A is right Only the transfer time differed, and the passage says “everything but the transfer time was held constant”, so it is the available explanation.

Why B is wrong The sand was the same in both batches, so it cannot explain the difference.

Why C is wrong The furnace was shared by both batches.

Why D is wrong Shape is never mentioned and would have had to differ to matter.

stem_html:
The observatory logged the transit at 3:14 in the morning ______ the second station, forty kilometres east, recorded nothing at all.

Which choice completes the text so that it conforms to the conventions of Standard English?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": ", but"}, {"letter": "B", "content": ", however", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}, {"letter": "C", "content": " but,", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}, {"letter": "D", "content": " however", "trap": "comma-splice-plausible"}]

Traps in this question

  • But, and, or, so — conjunctions take a comma before.

stem_html:

Which choice completes the text with the most logical transition?

explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • Evidence then a dated conclusion is causal.
  • The eleven years are the reason for the eleven-year window.
  • A contrast word needs two sides that disagree.

Why A is right The dating follows from the paper's single source and short window, so the transition is a consequence.

Why B is wrong Nonetheless marks a contrast, and the second sentence is the conclusion of the first.

Why C is wrong Meanwhile places two things in time side by side; nothing here is simultaneous.

Why D is wrong The date range is an inference, not an instance.

stem_html:
While researching a topic, a student has taken the following notes:

  • The Voynich manuscript is written in an unknown script on vellum.
  • Radiocarbon dating places the vellum between 1404 and 1438.
  • No proposed decipherment has been accepted by other specialists.
  • Statistical tests show the text has word-frequency patterns like those of natural languages.

The student wants to explain why the manuscript resists a simple dismissal as a hoax. Which choice most effectively uses relevant information from the notes to accomplish this goal?
choices_json: [{"letter": "A", "content": "Although no proposed decipherment has been accepted, statistical tests show the text has the word-frequency patterns of a natural language, which a random invention would not."}, {"letter": "B", "content": "The Voynich manuscript is written in an unknown script on vellum dated between 1404 and 1438.", "trap": "out-of-scope"}, {"letter": "C", "content": "No decipherment of the Voynich manuscript has been accepted by other specialists.", "trap": "reversed-relationship"}, {"letter": "D", "content": "Radiocarbon dating places the manuscript's vellum in the early fifteenth century.", "trap": "half-right"}]
explanation_html:
Traps in this question

  • The goal names an argument, so find the note that argues.
  • The statistics are the only evidence about the text itself.
  • One note supports the hoax reading; do not pick it.

Why A is right Resisting dismissal needs the reason a hoax is doubted, and only this choice gives it: language-like statistics that a random invention would not produce.

Why B is wrong A description of the object with nothing arguing against a hoax.

Why C is wrong The failure to decipher it is what makes the hoax reading tempting, not what resists it.

Why D is wrong An old date fixes when it was made, not whether the text means anything.
